# The `inlabru` workflow

## The syntax {auto-animate=TRUE .smaller}

::: {style="height: 50px;"}
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: "1,2,3"

# Define model components
comps <- component_1(...) +
  component_2(...) + 
  ...

# Define the model predictor
pred <- linear_function(component_1,
                            component_2, ...)

# Build the observation model
lik <- bru_obs(formula = pred,
               family = ... ,
               data = ... ,
                ...)

# Fit the model
fit <- bru(comps, lik, ...)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Components**

```{r}
#| eval: false
~ my_component_name(
  main = ...,
  model = ...
)
```

-  `my_component_name` how you label your component (.e.g, `beta_0`,`myspde`)
-  `main` input data for the component (e.g., a the name of a column in your data or a spatial object)
- `model` The type of model component (e.g., `linear`,`fixed`,`iid`,`rw1`,`rw2`,`ar1`, see `?INLA::inla.list.models()$latent`)



:::

::::

**linear predictor**

- can be defined within the formula:

```{r}
#| eval: false
lik = bru_obs(formula = 
                response ~  component_1(...) + 
                component_2(...),
              family,
              data)
```

-  or use a full stop shortcode after the componets have been defined

```{r}
#| eval: false

lik = bru_obs(formula = y~.,
              family,
              data)
```

# Temporal Dependence 



## Modelling temporal dependence {.smaller}

Data are often observed in time, and time dependence is often expected.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false
lakes = as.data.frame(greatLakes ) %>% mutate(year = 1918:2009)
lakes %>%
  pivot_longer(-year) %>%
  ggplot() + geom_point(aes(year, value ))+
  facet_wrap(.~name,scales = "free" ) + xlab("") + ylab("")
```

. . .

-   Observations are correlated in time



## Motivation {auto-animate="true" .smaller}


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

Smoothing of the time effect


$$
\begin{aligned}
y_t|\eta_t & \sim \text{N}(\mu,\tau_y^{-1})\\
\eta_t & = \mu = \beta_0 + u_t
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

The models we covered:

$$
\begin{aligned}
1.\ u_t&\sim \text{RW}1(\tau)\\
2.\ u_t&\sim \text{RW}2(\tau)\\
3.\ u_t&\sim \text{AR}1(\tau, \phi)\\
\end{aligned}
$$


:::

:::: 



```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false
greatLakes.df<- read.csv(here::here("datasets/greatLakes.csv"))

greatLakes.df$t.idx <- greatLakes.df$year-1917

Erie.df = greatLakes.df %>% filter(Lakes == "Erie")

pc_prior <- list(theta = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)),
                 rho = list(prior = "pc.cor0", param = c(0.5, 0.3))) 

prec.tau_e <- list(prec = list(prior = "loggamma",   # prior name
                             param = c(1, 1))) # prior values

# Model components
cmp =  ~ -1 + alpha(1) + ut(t.idx, model = "ar1",  hyper = pc_prior)
# Model formula
formula = height ~ alpha + ut


# Observational model
lik =  bru_obs(formula = height  ~.,
            family = "gaussian",
            data = Erie.df,
            control.family = list(hyper = prec.tau_e))

# fit the model
fit.Erie_ar1 = bru(cmp, lik)


# Model predictions
pred_ar1.Erie = predict(fit.Erie_ar1, Erie.df, ~ alpha + ut)

pc_prior <- list(theta = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01))) 

prec.tau_e <- list(prec = list(prior = "loggamma",   # prior name
                             param = c(1, 1))) # prior values


cmp_rw =  ~ -1 + alpha(1) + 
  ut(t.idx ,
     constr=TRUE,
     model = "rw1",
     hyper=pc_prior,
     scale.model = TRUE)

formula = height ~ alpha + ut
# Observational model
lik =  bru_obs(formula = height  ~.,
            family = "gaussian",
            data = Erie.df,
            control.family = list(hyper = prec.tau_e))


fit.Erie_rw1_constr = bru(cmp_rw, lik)


cmp_rw2 = ~ -1 + alpha(1) + time(t.idx, model = "rw2",
                                 scale.model = T,
                                 hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01))))

fit.Erie_rw2_constr = bru(cmp_rw2, lik)

pred_rw2 = predict(fit.Erie_rw2_constr, Erie.df, ~ alpha + time)



pred_rw1.Erie = predict(fit.Erie_rw1_constr, Erie.df, ~ alpha + ut)




dplyr::bind_rows(
      pred_rw1.Erie %>% mutate(Model = "RW1"),

    pred_rw2 %>% mutate(Model = "RW2"),

  pred_ar1.Erie %>% mutate(Model = "AR1")
) %>%
  
  ggplot(.,aes(y=mean,x=year))+
  geom_line(aes(colour=Model))+
    geom_ribbon(aes(fill=Model,x = year, y = mean, ymin = q0.025, ymax = q0.975),
                alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y=height,x=year))+
  facet_wrap(~Model)




```


## Gaussian Markov Random Fields (GMRF) {.smaller}

::: {style="height: 50px;"}
:::

A random vector $\mathbf{u} = (u_1, \ldots, u_n)^\top$ is a
**Gaussian Markov Random Field (GMRF)** with respect to a graph
$G = (V, E)$, with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and precision
matrix $\mathbf{Q}$, if its probability density is

$$
\pi(\mathbf{u}) =
|\mathbf{Q}|^{1/2}(2\pi)^{-n/2}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{1}{2}
(\mathbf{u}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top
\mathbf{Q}
(\mathbf{u}-\boldsymbol{\mu})
\right\}.
$$

The precision matrix $\mathbf{Q}$ satisfies the Markov property:

$$
Q_{ij} \neq 0
\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad
\{i,j\} \in E, \qquad i \neq j.
$$

Thus, conditional independence between two components
$u_i$ and $u_j$, given all the remaining components, is
encoded by zeros in the precision matrix:

$$
u_i \perp u_j \mid \mathbf{u}_{-(i,j)}
\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad
Q_{ij} = 0.
$$



## Discrete time models {auto-animate="true" .smaller}


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Random Walks**

- *RW1*: Assume independent first-order increments $\Delta u_t = u_t − u_t−1 \sim  N(0, \tau^{−1})$

- *RW2* Assume independent second-order increments $\Delta^2 u_t = u_t - u_{i-t} + u_{i-t} \sim N(0, \tau^{−1})$


:::{.fragment}

- Intrinsic model $\rightarrow$ sum-to-zero constrain.


```{r}
#| eval: false
cmp = ~ Intercept(1) +
  time(year, model = "rw1",
       constr = TRUE,
       hyper = list(prec =
                      list(prior = "pc.prec",
                           param = c(0.5, 0.5))))
```

:::

:::{.incremental}

-   Small $\tau$ $\rightarrow$ large variation $\rightarrow$ less smooth effect
-   Large $\tau$ $\rightarrow$ small variation $\rightarrow$ smoother effect
    
- PC-prior: $\text{Prob}(\sigma>U) = \alpha$ $\rightarrow$ penalize models with small precision or large variances (Baseline $\tau=0$).
    
:::

:::



::: {.column width="50%"}

**AR(1)**


- $u_t = \phi u_{t-1} + \epsilon_t; \qquad \phi\in(-1,1), \ \epsilon_t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^{-1})$



:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| eval: false

pc_prior <- list(theta1 = list(prior = "pc.prec",
                              param = c(1, 0.01)),
                 rho = list(prior = "pc.cor0", 
                            param = c(0.5, 0.3))) 

cmp = ~ Intercept(1) +
  time(year, model = "ar1",
       hyper = pc_prior)
```

:::

:::{.incremental}

- The precision $\tau$

- PC prior $\text{Prob}(\sigma > U) = \alpha$ (Baseline $\tau=0$).

-   The autocorrelation parameter $\phi\in(0,1)$:

    -  PC prior $\text{Prob}(|\rho| > u) = \alpha$  (Baseline $\phi = 0$ `pc.cor0`)

    -  PC prior $\text{Prob}(\rho > u) = \alpha$  (Baseline $\phi = 1$ `pc.cor1`)

:::



:::


::::



## Continuous time models


-   Sometimes the data are not collected at discrete time points but over continuous time

-   One solution (not a bad one usually) is to discretize the time (or covariate) and use RW model (`inla.group()`).

-   A different solution is to use a continuous smoother based on a continuous Gaussian Random Field (GRF) $\omega(t)$



## The SPDE {.smaller}


We define a (Matérn) GRF as the solution of a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE)

$$
(\kappa^2-\Delta)^{\alpha/2}\omega(t) = W(t)
$$


-   $W(t)$ is random noise
-   $\omega(t)$ is the smooth process we want
-   $(\kappa^2-\Delta)^{\alpha/2}$ is an operator that "smooths" the white noise.
-   $\kappa$ and $\alpha$ are parameters

:::{.fragment}
Approximate the solution (i.e. the GF) by a GMRF defined on a discretized domain or mesh using FEM.

$$
\omega(t) = \sum_{i = 1}^T\psi_i(t)w_i
$$
:::


:::{.fragment}


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}


The GF has a Matérn Covariance characterized by 

-   The range $\rho$
-   The marginal variance $\sigma^2$

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
    
Define PC-priors:

- $\text{Prob}(\rho<\rho_0) = p_{\rho}$
- $\text{Prob}(\sigma > \sigma_0) = p_{\sigma}$

:::
:::: 

:::



## Fitting a SPDE in 1D 


1.  Define a 1-dimensional mesh over the domain of interest 


```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# domain of interest 0-10
locs = seq(-3,13,1)
mesh1d = fm_mesh_1d(locs, degree = 1, boundary = "neumann")

```

2.  Define the SPDE model and the prior

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh1d,
  prior.range = c(10, 0.5), # Prob(range<10) = 0.5
  prior.sigma = c(1, 0.5)   # Prob(sd>1) = 0.5
)
```

3.  Use the SPDE model in a component of your model

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

cmp = ~ Intercept(1) + smooth(covariate, model = spde)
```
